# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

response:
This is a strong follow-up, and it settles several questions left open across the series. It answers most of the specific concerns I raised about the nine-month report, the Varga & Holm comment and the meta-analysis. Two points need more attention before its conclusions are fully secure. First, the "unplanned observation" in the control offices affects how the decline from nine to 24 months should be read. Second, the mediation result doesn't obviously reconcile with the trial's own hours and meeting figures.

## Arithmetic check

**Most figures hold:**
- **Timesheet per-hour gain:** 0.966 / 0.88 = +9.8% ✓
- **Log per-hour gain:** 0.966 / 0.89 = +8.5% ✓
- **Halden continuers:** hours 34.9 / 40.3 = −13.4% ✓; per-hour gain 0.968 / 0.866 = +11.8% ✓
- **Mediation shares:** 47 + 18 + 35 = 100 ✓

**Two need clarification:**
- **The Summary compares across measures.** "Fell from 12.5% to 8.5%" compares a nine-month timesheet figure with a 24-month log figure. The like-for-like decline is 12.5% → 9.8%, about 22%, which is what Section 5's "about a quarter" reflects. The Summary should use the timesheet comparison, or show both.
- **The counter cost estimate isn't explained.** Twelve percent more staff raising cost per contact by 9% implies staff costs are about 75% of total cost, or that the per-hour gain partly offsets the extra staff. The assumption should be stated.

## What this report resolves

- **Durability.** A controlled two-year estimate of +8.5% (3.4 to 13.8) on record-based output and log-measured hours meets Varga & Holm's own recommended standards. It rules out "entirely an artifact" for this setting, as I suggested a controlled long-run study would need to.
- **The meta-analysis's decay claim.** Its four long-follow-up studies were all uncontrolled and used scheduled hours. I had flagged that possibility as the reason a between-study comparison couldn't speak to decay; this confirms it.
- **Unrecorded work.** Logs show hours fell 11% against 12% on timesheets. Unclaimed overtime was real but small, about one percentage point.
- **Counter-office waiting times** are now reported against control (7.3 v 4.0 minutes), and the outcome is clear: the county ended the arm.
- **Baseline meeting data.** Treated offices started at 7.4 hours and control at 7.2. My earlier calculation assumed the arms began with similar meeting time, and these figures support that assumption.

## 1. The control-office meeting audit contaminates the comparison

The report treats the two control offices' meeting audit as a side observation. It is also a problem for the main estimate:

- From month 15, those two offices had lower meeting time and output per hour 4.1% higher than before. If the seven control offices are similar in size, the control average rose roughly 1 percentage point over the last nine months.
- **Part of the decline from 12.5% to 9.8% may therefore be the control group improving, not the treatment effect fading.** The report reads the decline as "consistent with some fading of an initial effect" without considering this.
- The audit probably wasn't independent of the trial. It happened after the nine-month report publicised the meetings finding, which is a standard spillover.

The report needs:
1. A sensitivity analysis excluding those two offices, or excluding their months 15–24.
2. The treated-office trajectory on its own, which shows whether treated offices actually declined.

If the like-for-like estimate excluding them is close to 12.5%, the fading conclusion largely disappears. If it remains near 9.8%, the conclusion stands on firmer ground.

## 2. The mediation result

**It confirms the earlier finding in the same offices rather than replicating it.** The hypothesis came from these seven treated offices at month six. The registered test uses the same offices, with new months of data. That is a genuine improvement on an unregistered correlation and largely answers Varga & Holm's "post hoc" objection. However, it is not the out-of-sample replication their objection was really about. "Survives a registered test" is accurate; it should be described as confirmation in the same offices, not as independent replication.

**The confidence intervals may be too narrow.** Office-months are not independent observations; the effective sample is 14 offices, 7 treated. With that few, an interval of 28–66% for an indirect effect is tighter than I would expect. The report should state how the intervals were computed, for example a cluster bootstrap at office level.

**The mediation share doesn't match the trial's own accounting.** Suppose log time covers the whole working day, including meetings. The similarity of the log and timesheet reductions (−11% and −12%) suggests it does. Then:

| | Log hours (approx.) | Meetings | Non-meeting hours |
|---|---|---|---|
| Control | ~37.9 | 7.0 | ~30.9 |
| Treated | ~33.7 (−11%) | 3.9 | ~29.8 (−3.5%) |

Output per employee fell 3.4%, and non-meeting time fell about 3.5%. So output per non-meeting hour is essentially unchanged. On this simple accounting, cutting meetings would explain nearly all of the 8.5% gain, not 47%.

There are several possible explanations:
- The mediation model estimates something different. It uses variation in meeting cuts across offices, not the average time accounting.
- Meetings produce some output.
- Log time is defined differently from what I've assumed.

Whichever applies, the report should state what log-in time includes and reconcile the two figures. If the accounting is right, it strengthens the authors' central point: most of the gain comes from removing low-value time rather than from rest.

**Mediator ordering.** Fewer meetings may themselves reduce fatigue. Whether the 18% fatigue share includes fatigue reduction caused by fewer meetings depends on how the two mediators were modelled. The Limitations mention unmeasured confounding but not this.

## 3. The Halden subset

- **The reverters weren't all coverage-bound.** The Summary says the three reverters all had "client-facing or coverage obligations." One was a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Under the meta-analysis's coding, deadline-driven work counts as *discretionary*. This suggests discretionary work can also fail under reduced hours, and that deserves a sentence rather than inclusion under the coverage explanation.
- **Non-response.** Fourteen of the 23 organisations responded. Non-responders may include more reverters or poorer performers. The authors' "upper bound" framing is appropriately cautious.
- **The attrition question remains unanswered.** With a Halden author now on the team, this would be the natural place to respond to Varga & Holm's finding that seven of the nine "preparation-phase" withdrawals happened after the schedule began. The report is silent on it.

## 4. Points still open from the nine-month report

- **Sick days (−27%)** are still not reported per scheduled day. If treated staff work fewer days, much of the fall is mechanical.
- **Resignations and appeal overturns** still have no confidence intervals.
- **Output per FTE**, the registered primary outcome, is −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2). The interval allows a loss of up to 8%, and the point estimate is lower than at nine months. "Mostly, not fully offset" is fair; the per-employee drift deserves equal prominence with the per-hour result.

## 5. The unplanned observation as a policy question

The authors handle this well. They say plainly that the trial can't tell whether reorganisation alone captures the gain or whether the hours cut is what makes reorganisation happen. Given the mediation result, this is now the most important open question in the series. A trial arm with a meeting audit or reorganisation but no hours cut would answer it directly.

## Where the evidence now stands

Across all five documents:

- **Discretionary, backlog-type work:** a real per-hour gain of about 8–10% persists at two years under rigorous measurement. Output per employee is slightly below control, between 0 and −8%. The gain has declined somewhat from nine months, though the control contamination makes the amount uncertain.
- **Coverage-bound work:** output per employee and service fall, and the one randomised arm was ended for that reason.
- **Mechanism:** removing low-value meeting time looks like the largest single contributor, possibly most of the gain, with fatigue playing a smaller role. Whether that gain needs the hours cut to happen is unknown.
- **Headline pilot figures (20%+)** were substantially inflated. The "entirely an artifact" and "no sign of decay" claims both went too far in opposite directions.

The most valuable additions to this report would be:
1. The control-contamination sensitivity analysis.
2. A reconciliation of the 47% mediation share with the hours-and-meetings accounting.
3. A response from the Halden side on the attrition reporting.
